This page goes with **Chapter 26, Voice Leading Triads** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/VoiceLeadingTriads.html). Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the rules. It builds on [Chapter 6, Triads](triads.qmd),
[Chapter 7, Roman Numerals](roman-numerals.qmd) and [Chapter 16, Figured Bass](figured-bass.qmd).

**How the page works.** Each example is drawn on a grand staff (soprano and alto on the treble staff, tenor and bass below), plays when
you press **Play**, and is **marked by a checker**: the same program that marks your exercises. A green *Right* is an example the checker
passes, a red *Wrong* one shows what the checker says about it. In the exercises the bass (and sometimes the soprano) is given;
type the other notes (`E4`, `F#4`, `Bb3`; **Up** and **Down** move a step in the key) and press **Check**.

## 26.1 What voice leading is

**Voice leading** (part writing) is the set of rules for how each voice moves from one chord to the next. Four things matter: each
part should be **independent**, each chord should be **voiced** well, the parts should move **economically**, and each part should be
**singable**. **SATB** (chorale style) puts soprano, alto, tenor and bass on two staves; **piano style** puts the upper three voices
in the treble staff and the bass alone in the bass staff. The model is Bach's chorales.

Two voices move in one of four ways: **contrary** (opposite directions), **oblique** (one holds, the other moves), **similar**
(same direction) and **parallel** (same direction by the same interval, a kind of similar motion).

## 26.2 Objectionable parallels

Do not write **parallel fifths** or **parallel octaves** (or their compound forms, twelfths and unisons) between any two voices: they make two
voices sound like one. Parallel 3rds, 4ths and 6ths are fine; parallel 2nds and 7ths are rarely used.

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="ok" data-rows='[["I","C5 G4 E4 C3"],["IV","C5 A4 F4 F3"]]'>Fifths and octaves do not move in parallel here: the soprano and alto hold the common tone C and the bass leaps.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="parallels" data-rows='[["I","E4 C4 G3 C3"],["ii","F4 D4 A3 D3"]]'>Parallel fifths: the tenor and bass both rise a step and keep a perfect fifth (G to C, then A to D).</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="parallels" data-rows='[["I","C5 G4 E4 C3"],["ii","D5 A4 F4 D3"]]'>Parallel octaves: the soprano and bass both rise a step, octave to octave.</div>


## 26.3 Voice ranges

Keep each voice in the range of the book's figure: soprano D4 to F#5, alto G3 to C#5, tenor E&#9837;3 to F#4, bass E2 to C4. (These are narrower than
real voices on purpose; the figure was read off the staff and the checker uses it as written.)

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="range" data-rows='[["I","G5 E4 C4 C3"]]'>The soprano's G5 is above the range.</div>


## 26.4 Rules of melody

Every voice is a melody. The book's rules, from Bach's practice: **tendency tones** resolve (7 up to 8, and, less strictly, 4 down to 3; 6
and 2 fall); **avoid augmented intervals**; a **leap larger than a 4th**, or a diminished leap, **changes direction** afterwards; and
**consecutive leaps outline a triad**. The checker flags the first two always (the leap rule as an error in the upper voices and a warning in
the bass) and warns about two leaps in the same direction that do not outline a triad.

## 26.5 Spacing, crossing and overlap

Keep **soprano and alto**, and **alto and tenor**, within an octave of each other. More is a **spacing error**; the tenor and bass may be
farther apart. Two more faults belong with independence of parts (the names are this site's): **voice crossing**, a voice below the voice
under it, and **overlap**, a voice moving past where its neighbour has just been.

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="spacing" data-rows='[["I","C5 G4 E3 C3"]]'>The alto (G4) and tenor (E3) are more than an octave apart.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="crossing" data-rows='[["I","E4 G4 C4 C3"]]'>The alto is above the soprano.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="overlap" data-rows='[["I","G4 E4 C4 C3"],["IV","A4 B3 C4 F3"]]'>The alto leaps to B3, below the tenor's C4 of a moment ago (and across it).</div>


## 26.6 Root position triads in four parts

A triad has three notes and there are four voices, so one is doubled. **In root position, double the root** (that is, the bass). Then
look at how the bass moves:

| Bass moves by | Upper three voices |
|---|---|
| a 3rd or 6th | keep **both common tones**, move the third voice by step |
| a 4th or 5th | keep **one common tone** and move the other two by step, *or* move **all three the same way** to the nearest chord tones |
| a 2nd | move all three upper voices in **contrary** motion to the bass |
| the same note repeated | keep the upper voices or rearrange them, keeping root, third and fifth |

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="ok" data-rows='[["I","G4 E4 C4 C3"],["vi","A4 E4 C4 A2"]]'>Bass down a 3rd (I to vi): two common tones (E, C), the soprano moves up a step.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="ok" data-rows='[["I","G4 E4 C4 C3"],["IV","A4 F4 C4 F3"],["V","G4 D4 B3 G3"],["I","G4 E4 C4 C3"]]'>I IV V I: a 4th up (one common tone), a 2nd up (the upper voices fall, contrary to the bass), a 5th down (one common tone).</div>


**The deceptive progression.** When V goes to vi (VI in minor) the bass rises a 2nd, so the upper voices would fall, but the leading tone must rise.
The book's answer: move the **third of V up by step** and the other two voices down, so **the third of vi is doubled**. In major, do the same only
if 7 is in the soprano.

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="ok" data-rows='[["V","G4 D4 B3 G3"],["vi","E4 C4 C4 A3"]]'>V to vi: the leading tone (tenor) rises to C, the others fall; the third of vi is doubled.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="leaptone" data-rows='[["V","B4 D4 G3 G3"],["I","G4 E4 C4 C3"]]'>The leading tone in the soprano (B4) must rise to C; it leaps down to G.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="leaptone" data-rows='[["V","B4 D4 B3 G3"]]'>The leading tone (the third of V) is doubled: never do that.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="doubling" data-rows='[["I","G4 E4 G3 C3"]]'>A root position triad doubles the root; here the fifth is doubled and the root only sounds in the bass.</div>


## 26.7 First inversion triads

Now the bass is the third, so look at the **doubling** instead of the bass distance. **Do not double the bass** of a first inversion triad: double the
root or the fifth, whichever moves most smoothly. Exceptions: a **diminished** triad in first inversion (such as vii&deg;6) doubles the **third** (the bass),
and in a run of first inversion chords the third is doubled in every other chord. Never double the third of V (it is the leading tone).

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="ok" data-rows='[["I6","C5 G4 C4 E3"],["V","D5 G4 B3 G3"]]'>I6 doubles the root (C), not the bass; the soprano rises a step, the tenor falls to the leading tone.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="doubling" data-rows='[["I6","E4 C4 G3 E3"]]'>The bass E (the third) is doubled in a major first inversion triad.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="doubling" data-rows='[["viio6","F5 B4 F4 D3"]]'>A diminished first inversion triad doubles its third (the bass, D); here the fifth F is doubled.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="chordtone" data-rows='[["I6","G4 E4 C4 C3"]]'>The figure 6 means the third is in the bass; the bass has the root.</div>


## 26.8 Second inversion triads and the six-four chord

**Double the bass** (the fifth of the chord) in a second inversion triad. There are three places a six-four chord is used:

- **Cadential**: I<sup>6</sup><sub>4</sub> to V, the 6 and 4 above the bass falling to 5 and 3 (the sixth resolves to the fifth, the fourth to the third).
- **Pedal** (or neighbor): I IV<sup>6</sup><sub>4</sub> I, or V I<sup>6</sup><sub>4</sub> V: the bass holds while the upper voices move.
- **Passing**: I V<sup>6</sup><sub>4</sub> I<sup>6</sup>, or IV I<sup>6</sup><sub>4</sub> IV<sup>6</sup>: the bass walks through by step.

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="ok" data-rows='[["I64","G4 E4 C4 G3"],["V","G4 D4 B3 G3"]]'>Cadential six-four: the bass G is doubled; E falls to D and C falls to B.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="ok" data-rows='[["I","G4 E4 C4 C3"],["IV64","A4 F4 C4 C3"],["I","G4 E4 C4 C3"]]'>Pedal six-four: the bass holds C while the upper voices move to IV and back.</div>

<div class="vl-ex" data-key="C" data-expect="doubling" data-rows='[["I64","C5 E4 C4 G2"]]'>In a six-four chord the bass (the fifth) is doubled; here only the bass has G.</div>


**Special situation: roots a second apart.** When two chords have roots a 2nd apart (IV to V, ii to I6), avoid parallel fifths by voicing each chord with the fifth
below the root in the upper voices.

## 26.9 Exercises

**One. Bass given: I IV V I.** Add soprano, alto and tenor: double the root in each chord, keep common tones where the bass moves by a 4th or 5th,
move contrary where it moves by a 2nd.

<div class="vl-exercise" data-key="C" data-hint="Add S, A and T above the given bass. Root position: double the root." data-rows='[{"rn":"I","B":"C3"},{"rn":"IV","B":"F3"},{"rn":"V","B":"G3"},{"rn":"I","B":"C3"}]'></div>

**Two. Soprano and bass given, with a vi.** The bass rises and falls by 3rds and 2nds.

<div class="vl-exercise" data-key="C" data-hint="Both outer voices are given: find alto and tenor so that each chord has its root doubled, and the leading tone is not doubled." data-rows='[{"rn":"I","S":"C5","B":"C3"},{"rn":"vi","S":"C5","B":"A2"},{"rn":"IV","S":"A4","B":"F3"},{"rn":"V","S":"B4","B":"G3"},{"rn":"I","S":"C5","B":"C3"}]'></div>

**Three. A first inversion chord.** In I6 double the root or the fifth; the soprano resolves the leading tone in the last bar.

<div class="vl-exercise" data-key="C" data-hint="I6 does not double its bass. The leading tone in the soprano rises to C5." data-rows='[{"rn":"I","S":"G4","B":"C3"},{"rn":"I6","S":"G4","B":"E3"},{"rn":"IV","S":"A4","B":"F3"},{"rn":"V","S":"B4","B":"G3"},{"rn":"I","S":"C5","B":"C3"}]'></div>

**Four. Minor.** In A minor the leading tone is G&#9839;; write it as `G#`.

<div class="vl-exercise" data-key="a" data-hint="Minor: the V chord has G#; do not double it." data-rows='[{"rn":"i","S":"E4","B":"A2"},{"rn":"iv","S":"F4","B":"D3"},{"rn":"V","S":"E4","B":"E3"},{"rn":"i","S":"E4","B":"A2"}]'></div>


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What the checker does and does not check
- It marks ranges, spacing, crossing, overlap, parallel fifths and octaves, the leading tone (doubled, or not resolved), the doubling for each chord position, complete chords and
  the melodic rules above. Rule by rule, with the chapter each comes from, they are listed in the header of `apps/shared/analysis/voice-leading.js`.
- **Site's readings:** the exact notes of the ranges (read off the book's figure), the names *crossing* and *overlap*, direct fifths and octaves in the outer voices (a warning: the book states
  that rule only for species counterpoint), and "no fifth only with the root tripled".
- **Not checked:** consecutive thirds and sixths, the "roots a second apart" voicing, the Mozart K. 331 exception, and whether the Roman numerals suit a melody. A clean result means no rule above is broken; it does not mean the music is good.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
